segments.text: In this video, I want to talk about building  reproducible machine learning pipelines and
why that matters. The deployment of a machine  learning model is the process of making our model
available in production environments where they  can provide predictions to other software systems.
When we develop our machine learning models,  we do so in the so-called research environment.
This is an isolated environment without contact to  live data where the data scientist has the freedom
to try and research the different models and find  out a solution to a certain product need. In a
common setting, we have historical data. And we  use this data to train a machine learning model.
Once we are happy with the performance of  our model, in the research environment,
we're ready to migrate it to the production  environment where it can receive input from
live data and output predictions that can be  used to make decisions. We often talk about
deployment of machine learning models when, in  fact, we mean deployment of a machine learning
pipeline. So what is a machine learning pipeline?  It is the series of steps that need to occur from
the moment we received the data to the moment we  obtain a prediction. A typical machine learning
pipeline includes a big proportion of feature  transformation steps. Perhaps this is even the
biggest part of the pipeline. Then it includes  steps to train the machine learning model and
steps to output a prediction. We create an  entire pipeline in a research environment,
and we need to deploy as well the entire pipeline  to the production environment. Why do we need to
do so? Well, because in the live environment,  we are also going to receive raw data as input,
and we need to transform it to create the  necessary features so that the model can interpret
them and return the prediction. When we deploy  our pipeline to production, we need to do it in
a way so that the pipelines are reproducible. What  does this mean? It means that if both the pipeline
in the research environment and the pipeline  in the production environment receive the same
raw data as input, both pipelines should  return the same prediction. Same data comes in,
same outputs should come out of both pipelines.  Why? During the research phase of our project,
we built a model, and we optimize its performance,  so it maximizes the business value. When we
develop a machine learning model, or a machine  learning pipeline, I should say, we test model
performance from a statistical perspective,  utilizing classical metrics like the accuracy,
the precision, recall, medium square error, and  any other metrics that you are familiar with,
and we also evaluate metrics that translate these  parameters into business value. For example,
we may measure the increased revenue that our  model will create, or they increase customer
satisfaction or any other measure that we're  interested in, and that will vary with the
organization. If we want to translate this value,  this revenue increase, for example, as I show in
this slide, from a research environment to the  real life, that is to the live environment, we
need to make sure that the live model reproduces  exactly, or at least as much as possible in
practice, the model we created in the research  environment. This is why our models need to
be reproducible. So why reproducibility matters?  First, if we cannot reproduce our machine learning
pipelines within the research and production  environments, we may incur in financial costs,
as I discussed in the previous slide, but we  also incur in substantial time loss because we
need to spend a lot of time trying to dig out  why the models are not identical or at least
very similar. And this will end up in the loss  of reputation of the team. But more important,
for me at least, is the fact that without the  ability to replicate the model's results exactly,
it is very difficult to determine if a new  model is truly better than the existing one.
When we develop a machine learning model, we  usually compare it with the current model or set
of rules that the organization is using. Without  the ability to replicate the results exactly,
it is very difficult to determine if the new  model is truly better than the current one.
